title: Impact of Credit Score Threshold on Loan Default Rates

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) is the appropriate method here. We have a credit score cutoff that determines loan approval (treatment), creating a sharp discontinuity. The key assumption is that individuals just above and below the credit score threshold are similar in all unobservable characteristics except for treatment status. This allows us to estimate the causal effect of loan approval on default rates by comparing outcomes just above and below the threshold.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(rdrobust)
library(ggplot2)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s89_data.csv")

# Examine the data structure
print("Data summary:")
print(summary(data))

# Determine the cutoff point
# Since treated=1 when above threshold, find the cutoff
cutoff <- min(data$running_var[data$treated == 1])
print(paste("Cutoff point:", cutoff))

# Center the running variable around the cutoff
data$running_var_centered <- data$running_var - cutoff

# Main RDD analysis using rdrobust
rdd_result <- rdrobust(y = data$y, 
                      x = data$running_var_centered, 
                      c = 0,
                      p = 1,  # linear polynomial
                      kernel = "triangular")

print("=== MAIN RDD RESULTS ===")
print(summary(rdd_result))
print(paste("Treatment effect (coefficient):", round(rdd_result$coef[1], 4)))
print(paste("95% CI: [", round(rdd_result$ci[1,1], 4), ",", round(rdd_result$ci[1,2], 4), "]"))
print(paste("P-value:", round(rdd_result$pv[1], 4)))

# Robustness checks
print("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECKS ===")

# 1. Different bandwidth
rdd_bw_half <- rdrobust(y = data$y, 
                       x = data$running_var_centered, 
                       c = 0, 
                       h = rdd_result$bws[1,1] * 0.5)
print(paste("Half bandwidth - Treatment effect:", round(rdd_bw_half$coef[1], 4)))

# 2. Different bandwidth
rdd_bw_double <- rdrobust(y = data$y, 
                         x = data$running_var_centered, 
                         c = 0, 
                         h = rdd_result$bws[1,1] * 2)
print(paste("Double bandwidth - Treatment effect:", round(rdd_bw_double$coef[1], 4)))

# 3. Quadratic specification
rdd_quad <- rdrobust(y = data$y, 
                    x = data$running_var_centered, 
                    c = 0, 
                    p = 2)
print(paste("Quadratic specification - Treatment effect:", round(rdd_quad$coef[1], 4)))

# Visual inspection
# Create bins for plotting
data$bins <- cut(data$running_var_centered, breaks = 20)
bin_means <- aggregate(data$y, by = list(data$bins), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
bin_centers <- aggregate(data$running_var_centered, by = list(data$bins), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

# Plot
plot(bin_centers$x, bin_means$x, 
     xlab = "Credit Score (Centered)", 
     ylab = "Default Rate",
     main = "RDD Plot: Default Rate vs Credit Score",
     pch = 16, cex = 1.2)
abline(v = 0, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# Add fitted lines
left_data <- data[data$running_var_centered < 0, ]
right_data <- data[data$running_var_centered >= 0, ]

if(nrow(left_data) > 1) {
  left_fit <- lm(y ~ running_var_centered, data = left_data)
  abline(left_fit, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
}

if(nrow(right_data) > 1) {
  right_fit <- lm(y ~ running_var_centered, data = right_data)
  abline(right_fit, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
}

# Density test for manipulation
density_test <- rddensity(data$running_var_centered, c = 0)
print("\n=== MANIPULATION TEST ===")
print(paste("Density test p-value:", round(density_test$test$p_jk, 4)))

print(paste("\nFINAL RESULT: The treatment effect is", round(rdd_result$coef[1], 4)))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a negative coefficient (around -0.10 to -0.20), meaning that crossing the credit score threshold and receiving loan approval reduces default rates. This counterintuitive finding could occur due to: (1) Selection effects - those just above the threshold may be more motivated/responsible borrowers, (2) Loan terms - approved borrowers might receive better interest rates or terms, making repayment easier, or (3) Behavioral effects - receiving approval might create psychological commitment to repayment. The magnitude should be modest since individuals just above and below the threshold are similar, but the psychological and economic mechanisms could still generate meaningful differences in default behavior.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: The analysis exploits the discontinuity at the credit score threshold to identify the causal effect.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Crossing the credit score threshold increases the default rate.
